source_refs.note: Book p. 262-263: heading printed 14.1.6; i, j, k, [x,y,z] = xi + yj + zk, Unit Vector, u + v in i, j, k, Examples 2-3, figure. Book error: Ex 3 solution prints u = 4i+6j+2k for v. Teaching notes ours.

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 14.1.6 (Book# 14.1.6). The book has no 14.1.1, so the portal numbers the sub-headings of 14.1 in sequence as 14.1.1 to 14.1.8; 14.1.5 here is the book's 14.1.6.
As in plane, we introduce three special vectors \(\underline{i} = [1, 0, 0]\), \(\underline{j} = [0, 1, 0]\) and \(\underline{k} = [0, 0, 1]\) in \(R^{3}\).

blocks.alt: Axes x, y, z from O. Short blue arrows i, j and k go from O to the points (1, 0, 0) on the x-axis, (0, 1, 0) on the y-axis and (0, 0, 1) on the z-axis.
blocks.caption: Unit vectors i, j, k along the x-, y- and z-axes (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: As magnitude of \(\underline{i} = \sqrt{1^{2} + 0^{2} + 0^{2}} = 1\), magnitude of \(\underline{j} = \sqrt{0^{2} + 1^{2} + 0^{2}} = 1\) and magnitude of \(\underline{k} = \sqrt{0^{2} + 0^{2} + 1^{2}} = 1\). So, \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\) are called unit vectors along x-axis, y-axis and z-axis respectively. Using the definition of addition and scalar multiplication, the vector \([x, y, z]\) can be written as:

blocks.text_alt: u equals x, y, z equals x,0,0 plus 0,y,0 plus 0,0,z

blocks.latex: = x[1, 0, 0] + y[0, 1, 0] + z[0, 0, 1] \\ = x\underline{i} + y\underline{j} + z\underline{k}
blocks.text_alt: equals x times i plus y times j plus z times k

blocks.text: Thus, each vector \([x, y, z]\) in \(R^{3}\) can be uniquely represented by \(x\underline{i} + y\underline{j} + z\underline{k}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
So \([3, -2, 5] = 3\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\), and \(2\underline{i} - \underline{k} = [2, 0, -1]\): a missing unit vector means that component is 0.
Think of \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\), \(\underline{k}\) as one step east, one step north and one step up; \(x\underline{i} + y\underline{j} + z\underline{k}\) says how many steps of each kind to take. \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) are the components.

A unit vector is defined as a vector whose magnitude is unity. In three-dimensional space the unit vector of the vector \(\underline{u} = x\underline{i} + y\underline{j} + z\underline{k}\) is written as \(\hat{u}\) (read as u hat) and is defined by

blocks.text_alt: u hat equals u over magnitude of u
u hat equals x over root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared times i, plus the same with y times j, plus the same with z times k

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does dividing by \(|\underline{u}|\) give length 1? Multiplying a vector by a positive number \(c\) multiplies its length by \(c\). With \(c = \frac{1}{|\underline{u}|}\) the new length is \(|\underline{u}| \times \frac{1}{|\underline{u}|} = 1\), and the direction is unchanged.
Use: when a question asks for a vector of length 5 in the direction of \(\underline{u}\), the answer is \(5\hat{u}\).

In terms of unit vectors \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\) and \(\underline{k}\), the sum \(\underline{u} + \underline{v}\) of two vectors \(\underline{u} = [x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}]\) and \(\underline{v} = [x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}]\) is written as:

blocks.text_alt: u plus v equals x1 plus x2, y1 plus y2, z1 plus z2
equals x1 plus x2 times i plus y1 plus y2 times j plus z1 plus z2 times k

blocks.title: Example 2
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} + 5\underline{j} - \underline{k}\), that is \([2, 5, -1]\).
To find: the unit vector \(\hat{u}\) in the direction of \(\underline{u}\).
Method: \(\hat{u} = \dfrac{\underline{u}}{|\underline{u}|}\); dividing a vector by its own length keeps the direction and makes the length 1.

Find the magnitude
\[|\underline{u}| = \sqrt{(2)^{2} + (5)^{2} + (-1)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{4 + 25 + 1} = \sqrt{30}\]
Why: the components are the coefficients of \(\underline{i}\), \(\underline{j}\), \(\underline{k}\); \(-\underline{k}\) means the z-component is \(-1\).

Divide by the magnitude
\[\hat{u} = \dfrac{\underline{u}}{|\underline{u}|} = \dfrac{2\underline{i} + 5\underline{j} - \underline{k}}{\sqrt{30}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{30}}(2\underline{i} + 5\underline{j} - \underline{k})\]
Why: multiplying by the positive number \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{30}}\) does not change the direction.

Check:
\[|\hat{u}|^{2} = \dfrac{4}{30} + \dfrac{25}{30} + \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{30}{30} = 1\]
So \(|\hat{u}| = 1\): it is a unit vector.

blocks.title: Example 3
blocks.problem: If \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + \underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\) and \(\underline{w} = -6\underline{i} - 9\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\), then show that \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) are parallel to each other.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + \underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\), \(\underline{w} = -6\underline{i} - 9\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\).
To prove: the three vectors are parallel.
Method: two vectors are parallel when one is a non-zero scalar multiple of the other. So we try to write \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) as multiples of \(\underline{u}\).

Write \(\underline{v}\) in terms of \(\underline{u}\) (the book's first line prints \(\underline{u} = 4\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\); it means \(\underline{v}\))
\[\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\]
\[= 2(2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + \underline{k}) = 2\underline{u}\]
Why: every coefficient of \(\underline{v}\) is twice that of \(\underline{u}\), so 2 can be taken out as a common factor.

Conclusion for \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\)
\[\underline{v} = 2\underline{u}\]
So \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are parallel (same direction, since \(2 > 0\)).
Why: definition of parallel vectors.

Write \(\underline{w}\) in terms of \(\underline{u}\)
\[\underline{w} = -6\underline{i} - 9\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\]
\[= -3(2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + \underline{k}) = -3\underline{u}\]
So \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{w}\) are parallel (opposite direction, since \(-3 < 0\)).
Why: every coefficient of \(\underline{w}\) is \(-3\) times that of \(\underline{u}\).

Hence
Since \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) are both multiples of \(\underline{u}\), the three vectors \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) are parallel to each other.
Why: \(\underline{w} = -3\underline{u} = -\frac{3}{2}\underline{v}\), so \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) are also multiples of each other.

Check: ratios of components.
\(\underline{v}\) to \(\underline{u}\): \(\frac{4}{2} = \frac{6}{3} = \frac{2}{1} = 2\).
\(\underline{w}\) to \(\underline{u}\): \(\frac{-6}{2} = \frac{-9}{3} = \frac{-3}{1} = -3\).
All ratios equal in each case.
blocks.answer: \(\underline{v} = 2\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{w} = -3\underline{u}\), so \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) are parallel to each other.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the first line of the solution of Example 3 the book prints \(\underline{u} = 4\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 2\underline{k} = 2(2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + \underline{k})\). The vector \(4\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\) is \(\underline{v}\), not \(\underline{u}\); the line should read \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 2\underline{k} = 2(2\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + \underline{k})\), which gives \(\underline{v} = 2\underline{u}\) as the book then states.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
\(\underline{i} = [1, 0, 0]\), \(\underline{j} = [0, 1, 0]\), \(\underline{k} = [0, 0, 1]\) are unit vectors along the axes.
\([x, y, z] = x\underline{i} + y\underline{j} + z\underline{k}\); the coefficients are the components.
Unit vector: \(\hat{u} = \dfrac{\underline{u}}{|\underline{u}|}\), length 1, same direction as \(\underline{u}\).
Parallel test: one vector is a non-zero multiple of the other.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Reading \(-\underline{k}\) as having no z-component: it is \(-1\).
Forgetting to divide every component by \(|\underline{u}|\) in a unit vector.
Thinking a negative multiple is not parallel: \(\underline{w} = -3\underline{u}\) is parallel to \(\underline{u}\), only in the opposite direction.
